label: Systems of Linear Equations
overview: A system of two linear equations is solved by finding the (x, y) pair that satisfies both simultaneously. SAT questions ask you to solve using substitution or elimination, determine the number of solutions, or find specific values (sometimes just x + y, not each separately). Recognizing when to use each method saves significant time.

keyFormulas.name: Substitution
keyFormulas.latex: \text{Solve one equation for one variable; substitute into the other}

keyFormulas.name: Elimination
keyFormulas.latex: \text{Multiply to make coefficients equal, then add or subtract equations}

keyFormulas.name: Infinite solutions
keyFormulas.latex: \text{One equation is a multiple of the other (same line)}

commonMistakes.mistake: Substituting into the same equation you solved from
commonMistakes.fix: When using substitution, always substitute into the other equation, not the one you just solved.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding instead of subtracting (or vice versa) when eliminating
commonMistakes.fix: If the variable coefficients are the same sign (e.g., both +2y), subtract one equation from the other. If opposite signs (+2y and −2y), add them.

quickTip: On the SAT, if the question asks for x + y or x − y (not each variable separately), adding or subtracting the equations may give the answer in one step.
